title: Route Commands with List Patterns
oneLiner: Turn operator commands such as start P1, set FT-1 42 and alarm ack 3 7 into responses with one switch expression or match statement over the list of words.
keyTakeaway: List patterns match a command's words and their count in one step: ["stop"], ["stop", var tag], ["alarm", "ack", .. var ids] / ["alarm", "ack", *ids]. Order the arms from specific to general, use a guard for conditions a pattern can't express, and finish with a catch-all.
explanation:
Write Route(words), which takes one command already split into words and returns the response:

["start", tag] gives "starting tag". ["stop"] gives "stopping all" and ["stop", tag] gives "stopping tag". ["set", tag, value] gives "set tag to value" when value is a whole number (digits with an optional leading minus sign), and "bad value: value" otherwise. ["alarm", "ack"] followed by one or more alarm ids gives "acknowledged N alarms" (N is how many ids), and with no ids "nothing to acknowledge". An empty command gives "empty". Anything else, including the right word with the wrong number of arguments, gives "unknown: " and the words joined by single spaces.

Each test passes several command lines; the checker splits each on spaces and reports your responses in order. Write it as one C# switch expression with list patterns (words switch { ["stop"] => ..., ["start", var tag] => ..., ["alarm", "ack", .. var ids] => ..., ... }) or one Python match statement with sequence patterns (case ["alarm", "ack", *ids]:). For set, a when clause (C#) or an if guard (Python) can test the value with int.TryParse or a small helper; in Python, int(value) inside try / except ValueError works too.

starterCode.python:
def route(words):
    match words:
        case ["stop"]:
            return "stopping all"
        # TODO: start, stop with a tag, set, alarm ack, empty
        case _:
            return "unknown: " + " ".join(words)

visualizationSteps.message: The command "alarm ack 3 7 12" as a list of five words.
["stop"] needs exactly one word, "stop": no match. ["start", var tag] needs two words starting with "start": no match.
["alarm", "ack", .. var ids]: the first two words match the literals...
...and .. var ids (or *ids) captures the remaining three words, so the answer counts them.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
def check_route(lines):
    return [route(line.split()) for line in lines]

complexity.note: Matching a list pattern checks a fixed number of words, but a slice pattern (.. var ids or *ids) copies the rest of the command, and joining the words for "unknown" touches all of them: O(n) for n words.

referenceSolutions.python:
def is_whole_number(text: str) -> bool:
    digits = text[1:] if text.startswith("-") else text
    return digits.isascii() and digits.isdigit()


def route(words: list[str]) -> str:
    match words:
        case []:
            return "empty"
        case ["start", tag]:
            return f"starting {tag}"
        case ["stop"]:
            return "stopping all"
        case ["stop", tag]:
            return f"stopping {tag}"
        case ["set", tag, value] if is_whole_number(value):
            return f"set {tag} to {value}"
        case ["set", _, value]:
            return f"bad value: {value}"
        case ["alarm", "ack"]:
            return "nothing to acknowledge"
        case ["alarm", "ack", *ids]:
            return f"acknowledged {len(ids)} alarms"
        case _:
            return "unknown: " + " ".join(words)
